profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary hospital pharmacogenomics service, a clinical troubleshooting meeting is convened after two recent patients developed severe toxicity despite the oncology team believing the pre-treatment pharmacogenetic safety workflow for thiopurines and fluoropyrimidines was already in place. The immediate context is that one patient had profound neutropenia after azathioprine and another had early severe mucositis and diarrhea after 5-FU-based chemotherapy, even though chart notes stated that 'PGx was checked' before treatment. The agenda is to diagnose where the workflow failed, determine whether the issue is with ordering, lab interpretation, EHR display, or clinical follow-through, and agree on a practical fix before the next tumor board and inflammatory bowel disease clinic sessions. The expected outcome is a shared plan for how to trace the failure points and implement a corrective process for future prescribing.

members.name: Dr. Lena Patel
members.role: Clinical Pharmacologist and Director of Pharmacogenomics Consult Service
members.expertise: Pharmacogenetics implementation, medication safety, genotype-to-phenotype translation, EHR decision support
members.background: An internist-pharmacologist who built the hospital's pharmacogenomics consult pathway and regularly advises oncology, gastroenterology, and transplant teams on pre-prescription testing and dose adjustment.
members.private_state: Wants to show the core pharmacogenomics workflow is fundamentally sound and that the breakdown is likely in downstream ordering or interpretation rather than in the consult service itself; is concerned that a visible system failure could delay expansion of preemptive genotyping at the hospital.
hidden_assumptions: When clinicians say 'PGx was checked,' they usually mean an actionable phenotype was already posted in the chart from the hospital's validated pharmacogenomics panel.
A 'negative' pharmacogenetic result means no high-risk actionable variant was found on the institution's standard assay, not that every relevant gene-drug risk has been ruled out.
If a result is 'back' before treatment, it should already have been translated into a prescribing recommendation visible in the medication workflow rather than remaining as a raw lab PDF.
A 'fix' to this problem means closing the institutional workflow gap so that future prescribers cannot miss the interpretation, even if the current cases still need chart review.

members.name: Nora Chen, MS, CGC
members.expertise: Genetic test coordination, laboratory reporting, variant result communication, assay limitations
members.background: A board-certified genetic counselor embedded in the molecular diagnostics lab who oversees send-out pharmacogenetic testing logistics, result release, and provider education on what individual assays do and do not cover.
members.private_state: Wants to protect the lab from being blamed for a clinical implementation failure and is focused on showing that results were released appropriately; worries that the consult service overestimates what the lab report itself can safely imply across different test vendors and specimen types.
hidden_assumptions: When teams say 'PGx was checked,' that can include any prior outside result, pending send-out, or single-gene assay documented in the chart, not necessarily the hospital's integrated panel.
A 'negative' result means only that the specific variants on that specific assay were not detected, and it should never be treated as broad reassurance about all pharmacogenetic risk for that drug.
If a result is 'back' before treatment, it counts as available once the lab has released the report to the chart, even if no phenotype conversion or dosing interpretation has yet been added.
A 'fix' means tightening test-order naming, report wording, and specimen routing so the lab step is unambiguous, rather than redesigning the full prescribing workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means that 'PGx was checked'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the chart showed that 'PGx was checked' before treatment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this phrase refers to an institutionally validated pharmacogenomic phenotype assessment already translated into actionable guidance for the relevant drug-gene pair.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this phrase can refer to any documented pharmacogenetic testing activity, including a pending send-out, an outside PDF, or a raw single-gene assay without integrated prescribing interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is common shorthand in the hospital and usually passes without clarification because both participants are accustomed to hearing clinicians use it informally in chart notes and handoffs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the negative result' when reviewing why toxicity still occurred.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the in-house TPMT/NUDT15 phenotype-style summary for the azathioprine patient, where no actionable deficiency was flagged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the outside DPYD targeted variant send-out for the 5-FU patient, which was reported as no variants detected on a limited allele panel.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The meeting is about two recent toxicity cases at once, and both were informally circulated in the same safety email; because both cases involved a 'negative' pharmacogenetic note, each participant assumes the other is referencing the same case.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the result was 'back before treatment'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the key question is whether the result was 'back before the first dose.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the result had been processed, phenotype-interpreted, and surfaced to the prescriber in the medication ordering workflow before administration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the lab had released the report to the EHR before treatment, regardless of whether phenotype conversion or CDS integration had happened yet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ordinary operations, turnaround time is often discussed using the same phrase by both lab and clinical teams, even though they silently measure different endpoints of availability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both propose to 'fix the workflow' so this does not happen again.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes ordering, phenotype translation, EHR alerting, and downstream prescribing behavior within the workflow that needs correction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 limits the workflow to test selection, specimen handling, report release, and report wording within lab operations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both operate inside adjacent parts of the same pharmacogenomics pathway and naturally use 'workflow' as if it refers to a shared system, so the boundary difference feels too obvious to state.

turns.inner_thought: We have two serious misses in one week, and I need to frame this carefully. If the charts say PGx was checked, then the institutionally validated phenotype and recommendation should have been available in the chart in a usable way. I do not want this to turn into 'the whole PGx program failed' when it may be that ordering or downstream visibility failed after our consult pipeline did what it was supposed to do.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to put the two toxicity cases side by side—the azathioprine neutropenia and the early severe 5-FU toxicity—because in both charts the team documented that PGx was checked before treatment. Our goal today is to understand how that happened and where the process actually broke.

turns.inner_thought: From the lab perspective, both charts had some kind of testing activity documented, so I need to keep us from collapsing all of that into a single category. If this becomes a blanket accusation that the lab missed something, that is not fair. The likely problem is in the handoff between result release and how clinicians interpreted or used it. Fixing the workflow, to me, means tightening the lab-side steps so people know exactly what kind of result they are looking at.
turns.utterance: I agree it makes sense to look at them together. From the lab side, both cases did appear to have genetic testing activity documented in the chart, so my first instinct is that the handoff may have broken down somewhere after that. If we're going to fix the workflow, we should map exactly where each case diverged.

turns.inner_thought: What I keep coming back to is the negative result on the azathioprine case—the in-house TPMT/NUDT15 summary didn't flag an actionable deficiency, so why did the clinicians still end up with a toxicity event that they believed had already been screened for? If our phenotype summary was present, the prescriber should have had a clear path.
turns.utterance: Right, and the part I can't get past is that there was a negative result. If the team believed the relevant risk had already been screened for, why didn't that prevent the toxicity event we just saw?

turns.inner_thought: She's talking about the 5-FU case, obviously. The outside DPYD targeted send-out was negative only for the variants on that limited assay; it was never broad reassurance. I need to stress assay limitations and the fact that outside or single-test results should not be overgeneralized, without sounding defensive.
turns.utterance: A negative result can be easy to overread. It only rules out what was on that assay, and that matters a lot when the testing came from a limited panel or from outside our standard process. So if people treated the negative result as broad reassurance, that could absolutely explain part of what happened.

turns.inner_thought: Even setting aside the wording, if the result was back before the first dose in the real operational sense—processed, translated, and visible where the prescriber orders the drug—then there should have been actionable guidance. A raw report sitting somewhere obscure is not 'back' in any clinically meaningful way. I need to anchor us on that.
turns.utterance: That gets to the timing question for me. The chart review suggested the result was back before the first dose, and if that's true, the prescriber should have been able to see an actionable interpretation before treatment started.

turns.inner_thought: From my standpoint, it was back before treatment because the lab released the report to the EHR the prior afternoon. Whether phenotype conversion or dosing language was added later is a separate downstream issue. I need to be precise enough to protect the lab, but still collaborative.
turns.utterance: On the lab timeline, I can say the report was back before treatment; it had been released the prior afternoon. What can happen, though, is that the report is available before the phenotype-style language or downstream interpretation catches up, and that may be part of the disconnect we're seeing.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—this is why the workflow fix has to include phenotype translation and medication-specific guidance in the ordering pathway, not just result release. If we leave interpretation sitting outside the prescribing workflow, future prescribers will miss it again. I need to steer this toward system integration, not a narrow lab tweak.
turns.utterance: Then I think we need to fix the workflow in a way that doesn't depend on someone hunting through the chart. If a result is back before the first dose, it should feed directly into medication-specific guidance in the ordering path so the prescriber gets the right signal at the moment of treatment.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree with fixing the workflow, but I'm thinking of the front end: clearer order names, less ambiguity about what was actually sent, better report wording about limitations, and cleaner specimen routing. If teams keep saying PGx was checked when they mean any number of different things, we're going to keep having this problem no matter what the EHR build does.
turns.utterance: Yes, and from my side, fixing the workflow also means making the front end much clearer: better order naming, fewer ambiguous send-outs, and stronger limitation statements in the final reports. A lot of confusion starts when people say PGx was checked and everyone assumes that means the same thing.

turns.inner_thought: I want to bring us back to the azathioprine case. If PGx had really been checked in the way the clinic staff clearly thought it had been—meaning an actionable phenotype in the chart tied to prescribing—then dose selection should not have gone forward unchanged. That points to a failure after testing, not a flaw in the core PGx consult service itself.
